dedupe_keys.name: impact of payment system design on tiering incentives in australia s rits rba rdp 2012 06

description: This case study uses simulation to test how the design of a payment system affects banks' incentives to tier, that is, to settle through an agent bank instead of joining the central system directly, which raises credit and concentration risk. It was written by Robert Arculus, Jennifer Hancock and Greg Moran of the Reserve Bank of Australia and published as Research Discussion Paper 2012-06. The study simulates Australia's real-time gross settlement system, the Reserve Bank Information and Transfer System (RITS), using a payment system simulator, tiering participants one by one and cumulatively under different liquidity-saving designs, and measures liquidity use, network effects, settlement bank and client credit exposures and concentration. Coverage is Australia's RTGS system. The paper is free online as a web page and PDF; RBA terms bar reproduction without consent. It finds some evidence that RITS's liquidity-saving mechanisms cut the liquidity cost of direct participation, which may explain low tiering in RITS compared with other countries, no clear link between design and the large two-way exposures that tiering creates, and only small concentration increases from more tiering. Caveats: it is a discussion paper with preliminary results and the payment data are not published. For simulation it shows how payment network structure shapes exposures and potential contagion, relevant to cascading failure studies of financial infrastructure. It is related to the Reserve Bank of Australia payments data record in this catalogue.
